Who is this Bhagavān, from whom sages did he hear, and how did you obtain this knowledge? In answer, Maitreya begins seven verses with “seated.” He was seated on the earth, in the lower world, with unobstructed spiritual power and unobstructed knowledge; he is superior to Saṅkarṣaṇa and to Śrī Vāsudeva.

Having shown the continuation of the disciplic transmission from Saṅkarṣaṇa, Maitreya now turns to the lotus-born Brahmā in order to describe the Lord’s manifestations. When the Lord was submerged in the one ocean, Nārāyaṇa closed His eyes while His consciousness remained fully present. He abandoned the sport of māyā and rested in His own self. At the appointed time, the power of time awakened Him for creation; the subtle karmic arrangement of the living beings then became visible to Him.

The lotus is called the form of the worlds because it illumines all the objects, qualities and experiences available to living beings. The one from whom it was born was Viṣṇu. O Lord, He entered it fully, without any loss of power, as its indwelling controller. In that lotus presided over by Viṣṇu, Brahmā became the creator, himself made of the Veda and endowed with the power to create.

Maitreya first describes Brahmā’s bewilderment to show that Brahmā’s power to create the worlds arose only through worship of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, not independently. Although he had taken shelter of the lotus grown from the water, he could not fully know the lotus, the principles of the worlds, or himself. The expressions of wonder and the description of the vast waters indicate the difficulty of the search.

The thought of the ignorant Brahmā is described: “Who am I on the back of this lotus? This lotus alone is here—where did it come from? Its support must certainly be below it.” After looking in this way he descended into the lotus stalk. The Upaniṣadic illustration likewise speaks of seeing the support while standing on the lotus leaf.

Through yoga that had matured, and through meditation on Bhagavān that had reached ripeness, Brahmā saw what had earlier eluded him—the lotus that was his own seat and foundation.

entries.sanskrit: किं च, आयामतो दैर्घ्येण विस्तरतश् च स्व-मान-देहेन मीयतेऽनेनेति मानम् उपमा शोभनश् चासाव् अमानो निरुपमो देहस् तेन । यद् वा, सुष्ठु अमानोऽपरिच्छिन्नस् तेन । यद् वा, ताभ्यां स्वानुरूप-प्रमाणेन, अत एव लोक-त्रयं सङ्गृह्यते यस्मिंस् तथा । विचित्राणि नाना-विधानि दिव्यान्य् अपूर्वाणि चाभरणान्य् अंशुकानि च तेषां कृता आसमन्ताच् छ्रीः शोभा येन, तेन देहेन विशिष्टम् । एवं स्वत एवातिरम्यत्वेऽप्य् अपाश्रित-वेषः स्वीकृतालङ्कारो देहो यस्य तम् अपश्यत् । यद् वा, केन प्रेक्षां क्षिपन्तम् इत्य् अपेक्षायाम् एवं-भूतेन देहेनेति संबन्धः ॥२५॥

entries.sanskrit: प्रेक्षां क्षिपन्तम् इत्य् अत्रैव पर्वत-रूपकेण निरूपितम् अपि विशेषणान्तरैः पुनर् निरूपयति । भगवान् एव मही-ध्रस्तम् । चराचराणाम् ओकः स्थानम् । सोऽपि तथा । अहीन्द्रस्य बन्धुम् । सोऽप्य् अहीन्द्राणां बन्धुः । सलिलेनोपगूढम् आवृतम् । पर्वतोऽपि मैनाकादिस् तथा । किरीट-साहस्रम् एव हिरण्य-शृङ्गाणि यस्य । सोऽपि मेर्वादिस् तथा । यथा पर्वतस्य गर्भे क्वचिद् रत्नम् आविर्भवति तथा आविर्भवत् स्पष्टं दृश्यमानं कौस्तुभ-रत्नं गर्भे मूर्ति-मध्ये यस्य तम् ॥३०॥

The mountain image is explained again through further features. The Lord Himself was a mountain supporting the earth and the dwelling of all moving and unmoving beings. He was related to the king of serpents, as a mountain is associated with the serpent-bearing earth; He was covered by water, like a mountain such as Maināka. His crowns and ornaments shone like mountain peaks and jewels.

entries.sanskrit: किं च, वन-मालया निवीतं कण्ठ-लम्बिन्या व्याप्तम् । आम्नाया वेदा एव मधु-व्रताः, तैः श्रीर् यस्यास् तया हरिम् इति पर्वतादि-रूपम् अपश्यत्, हरिर् असाव् इति ज्ञातवान् इत्य् अर्थः । सूर्यादिभिर् अगमम् अगम्यम् । स्व-व्यापारैर् आकलयितुम् अशक्यम् इत्य् अर्थः । किं च, त्रिष्व् अपि लोकेषु धाम स्फूर्तिर् येषां तैः । रक्षणार्थं परिक्रमद्भिः परितो धावद्भिः प्राधनिकैः प्रधनं सङ्ग्रामस् तत्-प्रयोजनैः सुदर्शनादिभिर् हेतु-भूतैर् दुरासदं दुष्प्रापम् ॥३१॥

He was covered by a neck-hanging garland. The Vedas were like bees, and Śrī was their honey; by that garland, the Lord was recognized as Hari. He was inaccessible to the sun and the other gods—impossible to grasp through their own activities. Brahmā understood that the mountain-like form was truly Hari.

entries.sanskrit: यदि अवं हरिम् अपश्यत् तर्ह्य् एव तदैव लोक-विसर्ग-दृष्टि संस् तस्य नाभि-सरसि सरोजं श्वसनं प्रलय-वायुं वियद् आकाशं च ददर्श ॥३२॥

After seeing Hari, Brahmā saw the scene of the creation of the worlds: the lotus in the Lord’s navel, His breathing, the wind of dissolution, and the ether.

entries.sanskrit: कर्म-बीजं लोक-सृष्टेः कारणम् । रजसा उपरक्तो रजो-गुण-युक्तः । अतः प्रजाः स्रष्टुम् इच्छन्न् इयद् एव नाभि-सरोजादि-पञ्चकम् एव । विसर्गेऽप्य् अभिमुख-उदत्त-चित्तः अव्यक्त-वर्त्मनि भगवति निवेशित-चित्तः ॥३३॥

The seed of karma is the cause of the creation of the worlds. Brahmā, colored by rajas and joined to the rajasic quality, desired to create the beings. His mind was directed to the fivefold object beginning with the lotus of the navel, and even during creation his attention was fixed on Bhagavān, the unmanifest source.
